newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Le Pen prefers left to centre-right win.
newsitem.headline: France's Le Pen prefers left to centre-right win.

text.p: French extreme-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen has said he would prefer the left to win a snap parliamentary election rather than the ruling centre-right coalition.

Le Pen, whose party is credited in opinion polls with 13.5-16 percent of the vote in the May 25-June 1 election, said on Monday night that a left-wing majority might obstruct President Jacques Chirac's drive for a single European currency.

"I think that would paralyse Mr Chirac in his project of dissolving France into the Europe of Maastricht," the far-right anti-immigration crusader told Europe 1 radio, referring to the 1991 treaty on European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"I believe we must at all costs refuse Jacques Chirac the blank cheque he is seeking for five years to aggravate the policies already in place," Le Pen said.

He said the electorate of Socialist leader Lionel Jospin was "more vulnerable" to the consequences of austerity policies introduced to cut public deficits and qualify France to join the planned single currency at its launch in 1999.

How National Front supporters transfer their votes on June 1 in constituencies where their candidate is eliminated in the first round may determine the outcome of the election if the race is tight between the left and the centre-right, polls show.

Despite Le Pen's attacks on the government, latest polls show more than half of his party's voters would back a centre-right candidate in a runoff, suggesting his influence on their voting behaviour may be limited.

Le Pen won 15 percent of the vote in the first round of the 1995 presidential election, but despite saying that Chirac was "the same as Jospin only worse", most National Front voters backed the conservative candidate in the runoff, polls showed.

In the current campaign, he has focused on the issue of corruption, charging that the entire political establishment is riddled with sleaze and saying corrupt politicians deserved to be hanged, as they were under the monarchy before the 1789 French Revolution.
